label: Constitutional and Institutional Architecture
info: Cultural heritage falls under the mandate of the Ministry of Culture, supported by apex autonomous bodies established in the 1950s: Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA, national academy for performing arts), Lalit Kala Akademi (visual arts), Sahitya Akademi (letters), and the National School of Drama (NSD). Regional propagation is executed through 7 Zonal Cultural Centres (ZCCs).

label: Key Flagship Publications and Portals
info: Sangeet Natak Journal (quarterly research journal of SNA); Lalit Kala Contemporary; Indian Horizons (ICCR); the National Cultural Audiovisual Archives (NCAA under IGNCA, certified under ISO standards); and the National Mission on Cultural Mapping (NMCM) implemented via the 'Mera Gaon Meri Dharohar' (MGMD) portal.

label: Theoretical Treatises and Classical Taxonomy
info: Performing arts are anchored in Sanskrit canons: 'Natya Shastra' by Bharata Muni (the foundational 'Fifth Veda'), 'Abhinaya Darpana' by Nandikeshvara, and 'Sangita Ratnakara' by Sarangadeva. Dance is structured into three essential facets: Nritta (pure, abstract rhythmic footwork and body movements lacking narrative), Nritya (interpretative dance conveying sentiment and theme via facial expressions and mudras), and Natya (dramatic storytelling with dialogue and characters).

label: Two Emotional Modes: Tandava and Lasya
info: Codified in classical canons as complementary modes: Tandava represents the masculine, vigorous, high-energy, and cosmic rhythm associated with Lord Shiva (Rudra Tandava, Ananda Tandava); Lasya represents the feminine, graceful, delicate, lyrical, and gentle movement associated with Goddess Parvati.

label: Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA) vs. Ministry of Culture Classical Recognition
info: Sangeet Natak Akademi officially recognizes 8 Classical Dances: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathakali (Kerala), Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kathak (Uttar Pradesh/North India), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), and Sattriya (Assam). The Ministry of Culture expands this list to 9 classical dance forms by including Chhau (semi-classical martial dance of Jharkhand, West Bengal, and Odisha).

label: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (ICH)
info: Inscribed performing and visual traditions from India include: Kutiyattam (Sanskrit theatre of Kerala, inscribed 2008), Mudiyettu (ritual theatre and dance drama of Kerala, 2010), Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan (2010), Chhau dance (2010), Ramman (religious festival and ritual theatre of Garhwal Himalayas, 2009), Buddhist chanting of Ladakh (2012), Sankirtana (ritual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipur, 2013), and Traditional brass and copper craft of utensil making among the Thatheras of Jandiala Guru, Punjab (2014).

label: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu) - Fire Element (Agni)
info: Oldest codified classical dance, formerly performed by temple dancers as Sadir/Dasi Attam; revived in the early 20th century by E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale (Kalakshetra foundation). Synthesizes Bhava, Raga, and Tala; embodies the Fire element. Hallmarks include the fixed half-sitting stance (Araimandi), dynamic geometric angular arm movements, crisp footwork (Adavus), and 'Ekaharya' performance (a solo dancer enacting multiple characters).

label: Kathakali (Kerala) - Sky/Air Element (Akash)
info: All-male classical dance-drama originating from temple rituals like Ramanattam and Krishnanattam, revived by poet Vallathol Narayana Menon through Kerala Kalamandalam. Embodies the Sky/Ether element. Renowned for stylized facial make-up (Vesham): Paccha (green, noble gods/kings), Kathi (knife/green with red streaks, arrogant villains), Thadi (bearded characters: red for evil, white for divine like Hanuman, black for forest dwellers), and Minukku (soft orange-yellow for women and sages); uses complex 24 basic mudras and minute eye/eyebrow choreography.

label: Mohiniyattam (Kerala) - Water Element (Apas)
info: Solo classical female dance named after the mythical enchantress Mohini (avatar of Vishnu); embodies the Water element through fluid, undulating, wave-like body torsions (Lasya dominance). Employs the characteristic 'Atavus' footwork, accompanied by Carnatic vocal music in Sopana Sangeetham style. Dancers don pristine off-white handloom sarees with gold-brocade borders (Kasavu) and an asymmetric side hair bun (Kuduma) encircled with jasmine.

label: Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh) - Earth Element (Prithvi)
info: Originated in Kuchelapuram village by Bhakti saint Siddhendra Yogi in the 14th century, evolving from Bhagavata Mela traditions. Embodies the Earth element. Distinctive for combining speech/singing with dancing (Vachika Abhinaya). Iconic sequences include 'Manduka Shabdam' (story of the frog queen) and 'Tarangam' (rhythmic balance dancing on the elevated rim of a brass plate, often while balancing a brass water vessel on the head).

label: Kathak (Northern India) - Storyteller Tradition
info: Evolved from temple wandering storytellers ('Katha Kahe so Kathak Kahave') and matured into royal patronage under the Mughal courts and the Nawabs of Awadh (Wajid Ali Shah). Notable for upright posture, complex lightning footwork (Tatkar) synchronized with ankle bells (Ghungroos), dazzling multiple spins (Chakkars), and subtle micro-expressions (Bhava). Governed by three primary Gharanas: Lucknow (grace, Bhava, and Thumri expression), Jaipur (speed, intricate mathematical rhythmic bols), and Banaras.

label: Odissi (Odisha) - Water Element and Sculptural Fluidity
info: Ancient classical dance mentioned in the 2nd-century BCE Hathigumpha inscriptions of Kharavela; nurtured by Maharis (temple dancers) and Gotipuas (young boys dressed as girls). Characterized by soft, lyrical torso movements and two core postures: 'Chowk' (a square, masculine stance signifying stability) and 'Tribhanga' (a feminine, tripartite three-bend body curve at neck, torso, and knee). Accompanied by traditional Odissi music and silver filigree jewelry (Tarakasi).

label: Sattriya (Assam) - Vaishnavite Monastic Tradition
info: Introduced in the 15th-16th century by Srimanta Sankaradeva and Madhavadeva as an instrument of the Ekasarana Dharma (Neo-Vaishnavite Bhakti movement) within monasteries called Sattras. Recognized as a classical dance by SNA in 2000. Danced to devotional compositions called Borgeets, accompanied by traditional acoustic instruments: the Khol (two-faced terracotta drum), Taala (cymbals), and flute; subdivided into masculine acrobatic 'Paurashik' and feminine lyrical 'Stri' styles.

label: Manipuri (Manipur) - Devotional Raaslila
info: Deeply woven with Meitei indigenous traditions (Lai Haraoba) and later infused with Gaudiya Vaishnavism under King Bhagyachandra (18th century). Focuses on the Radha-Krishna 'Raaslila'; lacks sharp angularities or stamping footwork, instead flowing in serpentine, figure-of-eight trajectories. Features the vigorous 'Pung Cholom' (dancing while leaping and playing the Pung drum), 'Kartal Cholom', and the distinctive stiff cylindrical skirt (Kumil/Potloi) adorned with mirrors and sequins.

label: Chhau Dance - Martial Heritage and Tri-State Variants
info: A semi-classical tribal martial dance deriving from 'Chhaya' (shadow/mask) or 'Chhauni' (military encampment), depicting episodes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and nature. Three distinct geographic sub-types: Seraikella Chhau (Jharkhand - uses highly stylized, symbolic masks); Purulia Chhau (West Bengal - vigorous acrobatic martial leaps using large theatrical painted clay-paper masks); and Mayurbhanj Chhau (Odisha - performed without masks, relying on direct facial expression and muscular agility).

label: Prominent Regional Folk and Martial Dance Traditions
info: Kalaripayattu (Kerala - oldest martial art system, involving weapons and physical strikes); Silambam (Tamil Nadu - martial art using bamboo staves); Thang-Ta (Manipur - sword and spear martial discipline); Kalbelia (Rajasthan - rhythmic snake-like movements by the nomadic Kalbelia community, using Pungi and Khanjari); Bihu (Assam - seasonal agro-fertility dance marked by rapid hand oscillations and pelvic thrusts); and Yakshagana (Karnataka - coastal open-air theatre blending vibrant costumes, heavy makeup, dialogue, and rustic high-pitch singing).

label: The Classical Canons of Indian Painting (Shadanga)
info: Codified in Vatsyayana's 'Kamasutra' and Yashodhara's commentary 'Jayamangala' as the 'Six Limbs of Indian Painting': Rūpabheda (knowledge of forms and appearance), Pramāṇam (correct perception, measure, and structural proportion), Bhāva (expression of emotion), Lāvaṇya Yojanam (infusion of grace and aesthetic charm), Sādṛśyam (similitude and truth to nature), and Vamikābhaṅga (artistic mastery of brushwork and color pigments).

label: Mural Painting Heritage: Ajanta and Beyond
info: Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra): 2nd century BCE to 5th century CE; tempera-on-mud-plaster technique depicting Jataka tales, featuring masterpieces like Bodhisattva Padmapani and Vajrapani. Bagh Caves (MP): Buddhist secular-religious frescoes; Sittanavasal (Tamil Nadu): 7th-9th century Jain cave murals; Lepakshi (Andhra Pradesh): 16th-century Vijayanagara mural art depicting epic scenes using dark earth outlines on temple ceilings.

label: Miniature Painting Schools: Mughal and Deccan
info: Mughal School: Initiated under Humayun by Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad; reached peak naturalism under Akbar (Hamzanama, Tutinama), Jahangir (mastery of flora, fauna, and realistic court portraits by Ustad Mansur and Bishandas), and Shah Jahan; known for fine shading and secular chronicles. Deccani School (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar): Distinct for rich jewel-toned colors, elongated human figures, Persian-Turkish cross-influences, and sensuous lyrical compositions.

label: Miniature Painting Schools: Rajasthani Sub-Schools
info: Mewar School: Bold emotional color palettes, deeply devotional (Ragavimsa, Bhagavata Purana). Kishangarh School: Celebrated for idealized portraits of 'Bani Thani' (painted by Nihal Chand under Raja Sawant Singh, marked by arched eyebrows, lotus-shaped eyes, and sharp profiles). Bundi-Kota School: Renowned for dynamic wildlife hunting landscapes (Shikar scenes) and lush, dense green foliage.

label: Miniature Painting Schools: Pahari Sub-Schools
info: Flourished in the Himalayan foothills (17th–19th centuries). Basohli School: Oldest Pahari style, marked by fierce primitive vitality, warm yellow/ochre backgrounds, monochrome architecture, and beetle wings pasted on paper to simulate jewelry emeralds. Kangra School: Rose under Maharaja Sansar Chand; famed for poetic lyricism, soft delicate lines, cool palettes, and romantic depictions of Radha-Krishna amidst undulating green hills.

label: Indigenous Tribal and Folk Paintings: Warli and Madhubani
info: Madhubani/Mithila Painting (Bihar, GI-tagged): Historically practiced by women on mud walls (Kohbar) and paper; uses fingers, twigs, and matchsticks with natural plant dyes to draw geometric patterns, Hindu deities, and nature without leaving blank spaces. Warli Painting (Maharashtra, GI-tagged): Tribal ritual wall art by the Warli tribe; paints on brown mud/cow-dung backdrops using white rice paste mixed with water and gum, using circles (sun/moon), triangles (mountains), and squares (sacred enclosures) to depict community farming and the circular Tarpa dance.

label: Indigenous Tribal and Folk Paintings: Scroll and Textile Traditions
info: Pattachitra (Odisha and West Bengal, GI-tagged): Cloth-based scroll painting coated with chalk and tamarind gum, rendered with fine black brushwork narrating Jagannath traditions and Krishna Lila. Kalamkari (Andhra Pradesh, GI-tagged): Natural dyed cotton textiles created either by freehand bamboo pen drawing (Srikalahasti style, illustrating temple epics) or carved wooden block-printing (Machilipatnam style). Phad Painting (Rajasthan, GI-tagged): Enormous hand-painted horizontal cloth scrolls (up to 30 feet) narrating folk epics of local pastoral deities Pabuji and Devnarayan, recited at night by Bhopa-Bhopi priest-bards.

label: Traditional Puppetry Forms of India (SNA Classification)
info: String Puppets (Kathputli of Rajasthan - wooden jointed figures controlled by strings; Kundhei of Odisha; Gombeyatta of Karnataka; Bommalattam of Tamil Nadu - combines string and rod mechanisms). Shadow Puppets (Tholu Bommalata of Andhra Pradesh - large translucent flat leather puppets casting color shadows on screens; Togalu Gombeyatta of Karnataka; Ravanachhaya of Odisha - opaque deerskin puppets casting black silhouettes). Rod Puppets (Putul Nach of West Bengal; Yampuri of Bihar). Glove Puppets (Pavakoothu of Kerala - heavily influenced by Kathakali costumes and themes).

label: Sanskrit and Traditional Folk Theatre Architecture
info: Koodiyattam (Kerala): Only surviving Sanskrit theatre tradition, performed inside temple theatres called Koothambalams, recognized by UNESCO; Bhavai (Gujarat/Rajasthan): Satirical open-air street theatre using the Bhungal wind instrument; Nautanki (Uttar Pradesh): High-energy musical verse drama centering on romance and bravado; Jatra (West Bengal): Open-air musical drama emerging from the Chaitanya Bhakti movement; Tamasha (Maharashtra): Energetic folk musical theatre featuring Lavani dance.

label: Contemporary Challenges and Cultural Preservation Schemes
info: Documented by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism, and Culture: Threats of craft obsolescence, loss of oral guru-shishya parampara lineages, economic marginalization of folk artists, and piracy of handloom/handicrafts. Countered by Schemes for Financial Assistance for Veteran Artists, the Guru-Shishya Parampara Scheme implemented through ZCCs, Geographical Indication (GI) registration under DPIIT, and the digital enumeration under the National Mission on Cultural Mapping (NMCM).
